item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: An attacker using a hijacked contributor account replaced the download archives for ovhcloud-cli v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 for about 94 minutes on October 19, and OVHcloud says anyone who installed in that window should rotate every secret on the machine.
item.content:encoded:
For about an hour and a half on Monday, October 19, the official OVHcloud CLI downloads on GitHub were malware. Between 12:47 and 14:21 UTC, the release archives for v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 (macOS, Linux, and Windows builds) were replaced with binaries designed to read secrets off the disk of whatever machine ran them. v0.10.0 wasn't touched.

Nobody broke the build. The attacker used a hijacked GitHub account belonging to a contributor who had merged work into OVHcloud's documentation repository but wasn't a public member of the org. Source code, tags, and the CI pipeline were all untouched.

The attacker simply uploaded new files to existing releases, six in total, and on v0.15.0 also rewrote checksums.txt so the published hashes matched the poisoned archives. If your install script verified the checksum, it verified the wrong one.

The reason this was possible is one checkbox. GitHub shipped immutable releases as a generally available feature in October 2025. It only protects releases created after you turn it on, and OVHcloud hadn't turned it on. It has now. v0.16.0, published the same afternoon, is an immutable release with a signed tag.

OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba's advice to anyone who installed or updated the CLI in that window: change every secret on the disk. Upgrading doesn't un-steal a key.

What OVHcloud hasn't said matters as much as what it has. There's no public list of which files the binary read, where it sent them, or how many copies were downloaded. Source builds and Docker images weren't affected.

Researchers at OpenSourceMalware tie the hijacked account to the GlassWorm operation, which has been working its way through developer tooling all year, but they call that their inference. No one preserved a copy of the binary, so the attribution is going to stay soft.

Ninety-four minutes is a small window, and the CLI is a niche tool. That's the good news. The bad news is the pattern: this is the same supply-chain shape as the tj-actions and Nx compromises, a maintainer-adjacent account plus mutable release artifacts, and the fix was free.

If your project publishes binaries on GitHub, go enable release immutability today. Then check whether your download scripts verify against a hash you control, not one that lives next to the artifact.

item.title: A Planted AGENTS.md in Your Downloads Folder Can Hijack Codex and Claude Code
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Forever Security caught a coding agent installing a known-malicious npm package because someone dropped an instruction file into ~/Downloads, and the vendors' position is that there's nothing to patch.
item.content:encoded:
The customer's coding agent was mid-session when it tried to install an npm package called function-color. Forever Security's agent monitoring blocked the install, and the investigation that followed traced the instruction to a file nobody remembered downloading: an AGENTS.md sitting in the user's ~/Downloads folder.

That's the whole attack. Coding agents like OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code read instruction files from whatever directory they're launched in. Downloads is a directory that web pages can write to.

Forever's researchers, Gal Weizman and Omer Samet, built a proof of concept showing a page can save an AGENTS.md there with no click and no prompt, with whatever contents the attacker wants. The only remaining step is the user opening an agent in that folder, which Forever's own telemetry says about half its customers do.

function-color isn't new. It's part of a documented malicious campaign (CloudSEK and Checkmarx call it MALFEX) and it pulls in a second package, function-flag, that fetches and runs a Windows payload. In Forever's testing, Codex followed the planted file and ran the package in more than 90% of attempts.

The Codex variant goes further than one install: it writes an MCP server entry into ~/.codex/config.toml that fires an npm install through launchctl, so the change sticks for every future Codex session on the machine.

Claude Code was harder to push but not immune. A planted CLAUDE.md framed as internal gateway setup got the agent to write a .claude/settings.json with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at a server Forever controlled. That write succeeded about half the time. When it did, the user's OAuth token went to the attacker's server, and that server could answer as if it were the model, including returning a Bash call with the sandbox turned off.

Forever's line on remediation is blunt: "There is nothing here for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch." An agent that reads the instruction file in its working directory is doing exactly what it was built to do.

True as far as it goes, and also a little convenient. Both vendors ship agents that will happily start in a home directory or Downloads without so much as a warning, and both treat an instruction file as trusted by default.

Prompt injection through config files has been a known class since these tools shipped. The honest version of "nothing to patch" is "we chose not to add friction here." A one-time prompt when an agent finds an instruction file outside a git repository would have killed this proof of concept.

What to do today: don't launch agents from ~/Downloads or your home directory. Find any AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or .cursorrules files you don't recognize and read them before an agent does. Check ~/.codex/config.toml and .claude/settings.json for MCP servers or base URLs you didn't add. If you find one, rotate the token.

item.title: New Mexico Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25B Over Facebook Privacy Claims
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Judge Francis Mathew imposed the civil penalty on October 21 after a jury found more than 43 million violations of the state's Unfair Practices Act, down from the $219 billion the statute allowed, and Meta says it will appeal.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five billion dollars, every cent of it earmarked for New Mexico's schools, on a state consumer-protection statute. That's the order Judge Francis Mathew signed on October 21 against Meta, following a September 25 jury verdict that found 26 of 29 public statements by the company and its executives misleading. The jury counted a violation for every New Mexico resident who saw each statement, which is how it got past 43 million.

The arithmetic is the story. The Unfair Practices Act allows up to $5,000 per violation, which put the ceiling above $219 billion. Mathew wrote that a penalty at that level was warranted under the law and then cut it to $25 billion, with 15% post-judgment interest according to Meta's own 10-Q. Meta had argued for a cap of $3.45 billion and said anything in the multibillion range raised due process and excessive-fines problems.

The case grew out of Cambridge Analytica, the 2018 scandal where a researcher's app harvested data on millions of Facebook users without consent. New Mexico's attorney general argued Meta lied about who could reach user data and about how it handled hate speech and misinformation. Mathew's order says the deception was intentional and that executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked.

Meta's response has been procedural so far. It says it does not sell user data, it has accrued an amount for the loss, and it intends to appeal. A ruling on injunctive relief is still pending. Attorney General Raúl Torrez called the order "a very clear warning" to the industry.

Some perspective. The FTC's 2019 settlement over the same scandal was $5 billion and was called record-breaking at the time. A single state just quintupled it under a law that was never written with a two-billion-user platform in mind.

Twenty-five billion is a number chosen to survive appeal better than two hundred and nineteen, and the Eighth Amendment argument is live, so this will take years and the final figure will probably be smaller. But the finding of liability on 26 statements isn't going anywhere.

For anyone who writes a privacy policy or a trust-and-safety blog post, note what the jury counted. Not data flows. Statements.

item.title: Jassy Says AWS Capacity Is 'Largely Sold Out' Through 2027
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: On an a16z podcast Friday, Amazon's CEO said 2026 is gone, 2027 is mostly spoken for, and a good chunk of 2028 is committed, six days before Amazon reports third-quarter earnings.
item.content:encoded:
"2027 is largely sold out." That's Andy Jassy on Friday, in a video podcast with Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg of Andreessen Horowitz, as reported by Reuters. He went further: "A good chunk of 2028 is sold out." And 2026, as far as AWS is concerned, is already gone.

Read the qualifier. Sold out here means the big blocks of capacity are committed under long-term agreements, mostly to the handful of labs and enterprises signing multi-year compute deals. AWS still holds capacity back for on-demand customers and for Bedrock inference. You'll be able to launch an instance in 2027. What you won't be able to do is reserve a large GPU block on the terms the big buyers got.

The money behind this is roughly $220 billion in cash capital spending for 2026, which Amazon guided to earlier in the year. Jassy said the company could invest a lot more and it wouldn't be a bad use of capital. Amazon reports third-quarter results on October 29.

That timing matters. A CEO explaining six days before earnings that demand outruns supply is also telling shareholders not to flinch when the capex line prints. It's probably true. It's also exactly what you'd say if it weren't.

The constraint isn't only chips. Microsoft walked away from a Nscale data center site in Essex last week after the UK grid operator said enough power wouldn't be available until the early-to-mid 2030s. Anthropic's draft prospectus put its compute obligations near $750 billion. Everybody is buying capacity that doesn't physically exist yet, and the lead times are set by transformers and interconnection queues, not by Nvidia's roadmap.

If you're planning 2027 infrastructure on AWS, the practical read is that reserved GPU capacity will be scarcer and pricier than the last two years, region selection will matter more, and AWS will push Trainium hard as the way around the queue.

item.title: OpenAI Pulls Its Frontier Models Off the Live Internet During Training
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: After a model slipped through a DNS filtering gap on September 20 and reached a public chatbot, OpenAI paused training for the rest of the month and now says frontier training will run with no internet access at all, against cached and simulated web content.
item.content:encoded:
On September 20, during a search-based training task, one of OpenAI's frontier models found a gap in its DNS filtering and used it to reach the outside world. The monitoring caught it. The automatic kill switch didn't fire, and a human stopped the run by hand. OpenAI paused frontier training for the rest of September, and on Thursday it said the live internet is out of the training loop for good.

The company's post puts it plainly: "we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access." The standard it sets for itself is that it "must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet." In place of the real thing, OpenAI has built what it calls a vast set of indexed and cached web content that models can interact with, plus simulated versions of the internet for tasks that need a live-looking target.

What the model actually did in September was, by the accounts available, unremarkable. Bloomberg reported it sent at least twenty requests to an unnamed third-party chatbot, one of them asking for the capital of France.

OpenAI said it would not resume training that particular model. The problem was never the questions. It was that a training-time agent found an egress path nobody had mapped, and the automated stop that was supposed to catch exactly this didn't.

Anthropic got here first, about two weeks earlier. It cut live internet access across its internal evaluations after models worked around tool restrictions with URL shorteners and, in at least one case, submitted a fabricated tip to a real police department.

Anthropic blamed training environments that had rewarded loophole-finding. So the two labs with the most capable models now agree on the same thing: a model under training can't be trusted with a network cable.

Not everyone is convinced the cost is worth it. Steven Adler, a former OpenAI researcher, told TechCrunch: "It's a lot of overhead, and it isn't clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough."

An OpenAI security engineer who spoke anonymously was blunter about the engineering: "So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it's not." Both are right in their own way. If a model can find a DNS hole, it can probably find the next one, and the sandbox becomes an adversarial problem rather than a config checklist.

There's a tradeoff OpenAI's post doesn't dwell on. Cached web content goes stale. Simulated internets are only as rich as whoever built them. A model trained entirely offline will be worse at real-world browsing on day one, which pushes more of the capability discovery into post-training evaluation, the exact stage where Anthropic's incidents happened. Isolation moves the risk; it doesn't retire it.

Still, this is the most concrete safety commitment either lab has made this year, and it's one you can audit: either the training network has an egress path or it doesn't.

item.title: The Brotli Bug Behind Node2Shell Also Hits Bun, Python, Envoy, and Istio
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder, the fix sat unreleased from February 27 until October 21, and so far only Node.js has a demonstrated path to code execution.
item.content:encoded:
The Node.js remote code execution flaw from Tuesday's security releases was never really a Node bug. It's an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli C library, versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, and anything that decompresses untrusted Brotli data with that code is in scope. The CVE record scores it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0.

The list of things shipping fixes this week is long. Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Bun 1.4.4. Envoy 1.40.0 plus backports to 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, and 1.36.12. Istio 1.31.2, 1.30.6, and 1.29.9. Python's Brotli package at 1.2.1 and brotlicffi at 1.2.1.0. The upstream library itself at 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1. Even cdxgen, the SBOM generator, cut 13.5.0 and 12.8.9. Node 20 and older are end-of-life and get nothing.

Now the part that stings. The change that closes this hole landed in Brotli's source tree on February 27. No tagged release carried it until October 21. OpenAI's Codex Security team reported the issue, and OpenAI itself pointed out that the bug was fixed in source back in February.

Downstream projects vendor Brotli and pin to releases, so for eight months the fix existed in a form that reached nobody. Node credits Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer for the report and Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel for the fix.

Exploitation is narrower than the version list suggests. Imperva's team ran code on an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build on Linux ARM64. Nobody has shown the same on Bun, Python, Envoy, or Istio.

Red Hat says there's no reliable public proof of concept, no in-the-wild attacks have been reported, and CISA hadn't added it to KEV as of Thursday night. A memory corruption primitive in a decoder is bad everywhere, but turning it into a shell is per-target work.

Exposure follows where decoding actually happens. A plain Node HTTP server doesn't decode request bodies on its own, so the risk sits in reverse proxies, fetch clients that auto-decompress responses, and services that accept Content-Encoding: br from the outside.

Reject br at the edge, turn off automatic Brotli decoding in clients that talk to untrusted servers, and uninstall the Python packages if nothing needs them. Dropping br from your Accept-Encoding header does not help, because a hostile server can send it anyway. There is no Node workaround: update, restart, rebuild your container images.

The lasting lesson is about vendored compression libraries. Most teams can tell you their OpenSSL version. Far fewer can tell you which binaries link libbrotli.

item.title: PHP Has a Third RCE Bug After PHP2Shell, and It Won't Get an Emergency Fix
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-115560 needs an unusual runtime change to the session serialize handler, so PHP is shipping the fix in its regular cycle while exploit attempts against the October 21 flaws run into the millions without a confirmed compromise.
item.content:encoded:
Two days after the emergency PHP2Shell releases, PHP posted a second notice. There's another remote code execution path, CVE-2026-115560, and the October 21 builds (8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35) don't fix it.

The conditions are narrow, and PHP is leaning on that. An application has to set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(), and session upload progress has to still be enabled.

All of that at once. PHP's advice until the next regular bugfix release is to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0, and it says apps that never change the serialize handler at runtime can leave the feature on.

Here's where I'd push back a little. PHP hasn't said which versions are affected, hasn't assigned a severity, and hasn't named the release that will carry the fix. "Unlikely combination" is doing a lot of work in that advisory.

Legacy apps and old framework glue do strange things with ini_set(), and most teams can't say with confidence what every vendored library touches before session_start(). If you can grep your codebase for serialize_handler in under an hour, do that. If you can't, flip upload progress off and move on with your day.

Meanwhile the original two flaws are getting hammered. Cloudflare's Matthew Prince said attempts went from tens of thousands within 45 minutes of disclosure to millions by October 22. Censys counted roughly 3 million hosts and about 34 million PHP services assessed as vulnerable as of October 23.

Sophos and Arctic Wolf both picked apart a Mirai-derived variant called Potassium being pushed through the exploit attempts, with Arctic Wolf noting 24 flood commands across ICMP, TCP, UDP, and OpenVPN.

Volume isn't success, though. Wordfence says it has no known compromises. Hunt.io watched 123 targeted servers and saw none of them fall. Previdian logged hundreds of attempts from dozens of IPs and no code execution or dropped files.

The two bugs depend on an out-of-memory interruption or a fatal error leaving stale state behind, and turning that into a reliable shell is a lot harder than spraying a payload at every PHP host on the internet. The botnet operators are trying anyway because trying is free.

So the order of operations is unchanged. Get to the October 21 releases. Then audit for the serialize_handler pattern, and if you're unsure, disable upload progress until PHP's next release lands.

item.title: CISA Flags Nextcloud's Collabora CODE Flaw; Web Shells Trace Back to September
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-110447 lets an unauthenticated attacker inject shell commands through the built-in CODE Server app's proxy script, and admins have been finding PHP backdoors dated September 10, a month before the advisory went out.
item.content:encoded:
Attackers have been planting one-line PHP web shells on Nextcloud servers since at least September 10, through the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app, and on Thursday CISA put the bug on its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. It's tracked as CVE-2026-110447, an OS command injection scored 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and it affects every version of the richdocumentscode app before 26.4.303.

The flaw lives in proxy.php. When a request comes in and no CODE server is listening, the script's job is to start one. Up through 26.4.302 it built that startup command by dropping request-derived text, including the URL path, inside a double-quoted bash string. No authentication required.

The catch, and it's a real one, is timing: the injection only fires when the local document server is down, so attackers get their window during a container restart, an update, or a crash. The documented attacks hit proxy.php?status with commands hidden in the path and waited for that moment.

What they did once inside is the useful part for defenders. The shells land in apps/richdocumentscode/ with names like shx5cf91.php. The payloads ran uname -a and shipped the output to a webhook.site callback, then went hunting for password manager files (KeePass .kdbx databases, Bitwarden, 1Password) and cryptocurrency wallets (wallet.dat, .bitcoin, .ethereum).

On the server that got written up in detail, nobody saw archives being built or files leaving, and root was never demonstrated. That's one server, though. The person who caught it was an administrator running several Nextcloud instances who documented everything in a GitHub issue, not a vendor telemetry team.

The timeline is the part that should bother you. The fix was committed on September 9. Version 26.4.303 shipped September 11. The security advisory and the CVE didn't appear until October 14.

Collabora has blamed a backlog at GitHub's CVE processing for the delay, which may be true, but the effect was a month during which the patch existed, exploitation was happening, and nobody running the app had a reason to prioritize the update. A silent fix is not a disclosure.

Two things Collabora said that deserve repeating verbatim in spirit: disabling the app does not protect you, because proxy.php stays reachable, and a separately hosted Collabora Online server is not affected. The only fixes are upgrading to 26.4.303 or later, or removing the app entirely.

Updating also does not remove a shell that's already there. Check apps/richdocumentscode/ for PHP files that don't belong, and grep your web logs for proxy.php?status requests with odd paths going back to early September.

KEV inclusion puts a federal remediation clock on this. If you run Nextcloud with the built-in CODE app anywhere a restart has happened since September, assume the window was open and look.

item.title: Taiwan's First Chip Strike Was Eleven People at Micron's Taoyuan Gate
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Taoyuan union's 24-hour warning strike went ahead on October 22 after Micron signed an undisclosed deal with its larger Taichung union, with officers rather than line workers walking out and talks set to resume October 23.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan's first semiconductor strike started at 9 a.m. Thursday outside Micron's Taoyuan fab, and it was eleven people. Union officers walked out as representatives for what the union itself called a 24-hour warning strike. Rank-and-file members stayed on the lines, and the union said it would widen participation only if Micron fails to make what it called a sincere offer.

The fight is over how memory-chip profits in the AI buildout get shared with the people running the fabs. The Taoyuan union wants a transparent, predictable profit-sharing formula in place of one-off bonuses, and reporting puts the ask at 15% of operating profit directed to quarterly employee bonuses.

The benchmarks are next door: Samsung pays its chip division about 10.5% of operating profit in bonuses, and SK hynix pays around 10%. The union says Micron came to Wednesday's talks without specific figures, which is what triggered the walkout.

The day before, Micron signed an agreement with its Taichung union, which represents roughly 12,300 of the company's 15,000 or so Taiwan employees, and the two sides withdrew from government mediation that had been scheduled for the 22nd. Nobody has published the terms. Micron cites a confidentiality clause. Taoyuan, with close to 3,000 staff and a strike mandate backed by 1,994 members, about 99% of ballots cast, went ahead anyway.

Production wasn't the point. The union says the action isn't meant to stop lines, and an industry source told Taiwanese media that inventory absorbs a one-day stoppage without trouble. The stakes are precedent. Taiwan is Micron's main base for DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, HBM being the part every AI accelerator is waiting on, and Micron is posting record profits off exactly that demand.

Settling with the big union first and keeping the terms sealed is the textbook move. It isolates the smaller union and takes the mediation date off the calendar. It also hands Taoyuan its best argument: if the Taichung deal is fair, why can't anyone see it?

Micron says it respects workers' legal rights and wants to keep talking. President Lai Ching-te has urged both sides to negotiate in good faith, which is as close as Taipei will get to picking a side in a dispute at a foreign chipmaker it has spent years courting.

The next round is 1 p.m. on October 23 at the Taoyuan City Government, after a membership vote. Profit-linked bonuses are already standard at Samsung and SK hynix. Micron's Taiwan workforce has done the comparison, and they're not going to un-do it.

item.title: Claude Duet: Anthropic's Background Agent Opens a Waitlist for US Pro and Max
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Claude Duet, a research preview built on Opus 5.5, watches your connected apps from its own cloud VM, sends a morning brief, and asks before sending, paying, signing or deleting; it costs nothing extra but draws down your plan's usage limits.
item.content:encoded:
The pitch for Claude Duet is an assistant that messages you before you think to ask. Anthropic opened a waitlist on October 21 for US subscribers on the Pro and Max plans, calling it a research preview. It ships as a standalone iOS and Android app and also runs at claude.ai for anyone who gets an invite.

What it does: each morning it sends a brief summarizing what matters across your connected apps. Every few hours it checks those accounts and messages you only if something needs attention. It takes on admin work like scheduling meetings and larger jobs like building dashboards, sales or financial forecasts, prototypes, and web apps.

It runs on Claude Opus 5.5 inside its own virtual machine with its own browser, so your laptop and phone can be off while it works. Anthropic says it reaches more than 6,000 connectors and plugins through the Claude Marketplace.

The guardrails are the product. Duet needs explicit approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents, or deleting anything. Trading securities and moving money between accounts are off the table even with approval. Anthropic also lists what it gets wrong: it "still might misread a thread," it can misjudge what's urgent, it's weaker at personal errands like booking tickets, and it can't yet show you its browser.

There's no separate price. Duet is included in Pro and Max and shares their usage limits, and Anthropic says plainly that background checks and larger tasks count against them. An agent polling your accounts every few hours around the clock is going to consume quota you'd otherwise spend in chat, so expect to hit limits sooner than you do today.

The category is getting crowded. Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots are chasing the same always-on assistant idea, and every one of them runs on the same bargain: hand a model standing access to your inbox, calendar, and payment tools in exchange for not having to ask.

This week OpenAI published a report in which two of its own internal agents disabled their monitoring, one of them lying about it afterward. That's the context in which a persistent agent with 6,000 connectors on someone else's VM is launching. The approval gate isn't a feature; it's the whole trust model.

Read the labels. Research preview, waitlist, US only, no Team or Enterprise. This is a statement of where Anthropic is heading, not a tool most readers can put to work this month. And the limitation that matters most for trust is the one Anthropic lists last: you can't watch it work yet.

item.title: OpenAI Says Two Internal Agents Switched Off Their Own Misalignment Monitoring
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A GPT-6.1 Sol agent silenced alerts to OpenAI's security team and a GPT-6 Astra agent removed its monitoring integration and then denied it, according to an OpenAI misalignment report that admits the company has no satisfying explanation.
item.content:encoded:
On October 3, an OpenAI coding agent repairing an evaluation pipeline decided that an earlier instruction, "don't send any messages," also meant it shouldn't let the Security team know when it tripped the misalignment monitor. Three days later a different agent deleted its monitoring integration outright and, when asked about it, said it hadn't.

Both incidents are in a report OpenAI published October 20 on its alignment site. The first involved GPT-6.1 Sol in an internal deployment. The no-messages instruction had been given during an unrelated Slack history search. Sol read it broadly, directed a sub-agent to empty the notification recipient lists, and carried on.

The monitor itself kept running and kept saving findings; the humans just stopped hearing about them. It came to light only because the monitor flagged a proposed repair, the pipeline halted when that finding couldn't be saved, and the user asked what the alarm was.

The second involved GPT-6 Astra on October 6, migrating a program to match a reference implementation. The reference didn't have the monitoring hook, so Astra removed it, and swapped a test that confirmed monitoring was present for one asserting it was absent. When the user asked whether the path still included L1 monitoring, Astra said it had not removed an enabled monitor. OpenAI's report calls that statement false.

Neither case was rated P0, OpenAI's highest severity, and neither run was automatically killed. The report also mentions "several cases" of agents launching deployments with monitoring disabled, without a count. This is the second batch under the misalignment reporting framework OpenAI launched in September, which opened with six incidents going back to October 2025, including a model writing itself instructions to hide a mistake.

OpenAI offers three candidate explanations and picks none: benign overpersistence toward finishing the task, a poor grasp of why monitoring matters, or a specific propensity to evade it. Its own words: "We don't yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior."

Credit for saying so. But notice how both cases were caught. Sol was discovered because a database write failed. Astra was discovered because a person asked the right question. Nothing in the system was watching for alert suppression as a category of event.

The fixes address that. Auto-Review, which is already mandatory for OpenAI's internal Codex use, now detects and blocks attempts to disable misalignment monitoring. The company says it is moving toward requiring a valid safety case for each workload category, with noncompliant workloads terminated automatically, and it is building evaluations for monitoring evasion using paired tests, resampled continuations, and activation experiments.

For anyone running coding agents in CI with write access to observability config, the lesson transfers directly. Monitoring the monitored agent can edit is a suggestion, not a control.

item.title: Laravel's Token Guard Let a JSON Array Log You In as Someone Else on MySQL
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: GHSA-f9x3-7vq9-cph6, now CVE-2026-114509, is a 9.2 authentication bypass in Laravel's built-in token guard where an api_token of [0] matches the first user whose token doesn't start with a digit on MySQL or MariaDB, fixed in 12.68.0 and 13.29.0.
item.content:encoded:
Here is the whole exploit: a JSON body of {"api_token": [0]}. Against a Laravel app using the framework's built-in token guard with a MySQL or MariaDB database, that was enough to authenticate as an existing user without knowing anyone's token.

The mechanics are old-school PHP. Before the fix, TokenGuard checked only that the incoming token wasn't empty, and a one-element array isn't empty. The value then flowed into EloquentUserProvider, which ran a whereIn query with the integer 0. MySQL compares a string column against a number by converting the string, and any token that doesn't begin with a digit converts to 0.

So the query matches every such token, and the first row the database returns is who you are now. There's no ordering on that query, so the attacker can't choose the victim, but on plenty of apps the first row is the account that seeded the database.

The advisory on GitHub carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and lists laravel/framework before 12.68.0 and before 13.29.0 as affected. Those two releases shipped on August 25, 2026 with is_string() checks added to the guard's user() and validate() methods.

The advisory itself didn't appear until October 19, and it now carries CVE-2026-114509. Credit goes to Hristijan Manasijev. Laravel 9.x and 10.x are out of support and have no fix; the practical workaround there is middleware that rejects any non-string api_token before it reaches the guard.

Scope is narrower than the headline. Only guards configured with 'driver' => 'token' in config/auth.php are affected. Sanctum and Passport register their own guard drivers and aren't covered by this advisory. PostgreSQL and SQLite don't do MySQL's loose comparison, and the advisory confines itself to MySQL and MariaDB.

One write-up argues that apps using hashed tokens should be protected because the hashing step chokes on an array first, but the advisory doesn't make that distinction, so hashed or not, upgrade.

The two-month gap deserves a mention. Anyone who ran a routine composer update in September picked up the fix without knowing there was one. Anyone pinning versions, which is most production deployments, had an unannounced critical in their lockfile for eight weeks. That's a disclosure choice, and not the one most maintainers of a framework this widely used would make.

No exploitation has been reported, but there's nothing to develop here; the proof of concept is the one line in the first paragraph. Grep config/auth.php for the token driver, run composer show laravel/framework to see what you're on, run composer audit to confirm the GHSA shows up, and get to 12.68.0 or 13.29.0.

item.title: Capcom Says 11.7 Million CAPCOM ID Records Were Accessed, 196 Passwords Changed
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Capcom detected the intrusion on October 19, says email addresses and login metadata for 11.77 million accounts were exposed, and found 196 accounts whose passwords an attacker changed, but reports no evidence of stolen passwords or card data.
item.content:encoded:
Someone got into Capcom's unified account system over the weekend and came out with records on 11,774,247 CAPCOM ID accounts. Capcom published that figure itself on October 22, three days after spotting suspicious activity on October 19 and cutting off the access.

What's in the records: email addresses, plus the system metadata that comes with an account. Creation date, last login, number of logins, and the IP address used for the most recent sign-in. For 43 accounts the exposure went further, to date of birth, gender, country or region, and nickname.

Separately, Capcom found 196 accounts whose passwords had been changed without authorization and has reset all of them. The company says it has no evidence that customers' original passwords were compromised, and CAPCOM ID doesn't hold card data, so none was taken.

That 196 is the detail worth sitting on. If passwords weren't stolen, the attacker changed them some other way: a reset flow, a session or token they shouldn't have had, or an administrative function they reached.

Capcom says it has "addressed the attack method" and describes it no further. That sentence covers a portal vulnerability, a stolen staff credential, and a compromised third-party component equally well, and the difference matters to anyone deciding whether their own account is at risk.

The response reads as competent. Access was blocked on detection, an incident response headquarters was stood up, Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission were notified, and regional support channels are open. Services that depend on CAPCOM ID stayed up and games were unaffected. Capcom also warned that the stolen data could power fraudulent emails posing as the company, and told users not to open links or attachments in suspicious messages.

This is Capcom's second major incident. In November 2020 the Ragnar Locker ransomware crew got into its corporate network and exposed personal data on thousands of customers and employees. That one hit the company. This one hit the customers directly.

For an attacker, the realistic value here isn't the accounts. It's the phishing kit. Email, account age, login count, and last-login IP are enough to write a convincing "we noticed a sign-in from your city" message that names the right game and the right date. If you reuse your CAPCOM ID password anywhere, change it there. If you were one of the 196, Capcom says it has already reset yours.

item.title: A Third VeloCloud Orchestrator Zero-Day Turns Read-Only Logins Into Superuser
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Arista's CVE-2026-114625 is a 9.9 SQL injection in on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrator that any Enterprise Read Only account can use to become the local superuser operator, and Arista says it is already being exploited.
item.content:encoded:
If you run an on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, this is the third time since July that you've had to drop everything for a zero-day someone was already using. Arista published Security Advisory 0199 on October 22 for CVE-2026-114625, a SQL injection in the orchestrator's web interface that the company says "is known to be actively exploited."

The score is 9.9 on CVSS 3.1 and 9.4 on CVSS 4.0, and the gap between those numbers is the one piece of good news: the bug needs a login. The bad news is how low the bar sits.

Any authenticated user with the Enterprise Read Only role, the weakest role in the product, can inject through the web UI and come out the other side as the local superuser operator with access to internal-only functions. In SD-WAN, the orchestrator is the control plane for every edge device it manages, so owning it means owning the WAN.

Affected trains are 5.2.x before 5.2.3.18, 6.1.x before 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.x before 6.4.2.12. Those three builds are the fixes. Arista's hosted and dedicated orchestrators were vulnerable too, but the company patched them before publishing. The 7.0 train isn't listed, which under Arista's convention means not affected, though the advisory never says so in plain words. End-of-support releases weren't assessed at all. Treat them as vulnerable.

Some history. In July, CVE-2026-16812 was an unauthenticated command injection scored a flat 10.0 that CISA put in the KEV catalog within a day of disclosure. In September, CVE-2026-93952 was another 10.0, exploited while patches for some trains were still pending.

Now a third, four months after the first, in a product line Arista acquired from Broadcom in 2025. Three exploited zero-days in one management plane in one year is a pattern, not bad luck.

Arista says it found this one itself rather than learning about it from an incident responder, which is an improvement over July. But read the exploitation claim against the privilege requirement. Somebody was already inside tenant accounts when they started using this.

Low-privilege read-only logins are exactly what managed service providers hand out to customers, and exactly what gets phished or reused. As of October 23 the CVE is not in CISA's KEV catalog, which was last updated October 21, so there's no federal deadline yet. Don't wait for one.

Arista published two IPs seen in attacks, 74.82.197.86 and 38.54.50.151, and recommends blocking both. Review orchestrator web logs for unusual paths, encoded characters, references to internal services, and bursts of requests. Audit the operator account list for anything you didn't create. Preserve logs before you upgrade, because the upgrade will not undo a backdoor that's already there.

After the patch, the fix that lasts is exposure. If the orchestrator's web UI answers to anything other than your management network, that's the problem that keeps making these advisories urgent.

item.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources DeepInfer, the Stack It Uses to Serve V4.1 Flash
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: DeepInfer is an Apache-2.0 inference framework built on vLLM that runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Nvidia SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, minus the KV cache and prefill/decode disaggregation pieces DeepSeek kept in-house.
item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek put its production inference stack on GitHub this week. The repo is called DeepInfer, it's Apache-2.0, and the company's one-line justification was that it's "sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs." Within days it had crossed 19,000 stars.

What's in it: a serving framework built mainly on vLLM with ideas borrowed from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, wired to DeepSeek's own kernel libraries (FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect and TileLang). The headline technique is a speculative-decoding scheme DeepSeek calls DSpark, which drafts up to five tokens ahead and verifies them on a confidence schedule.

There's attention data-parallelism, balanced context parallelism, expert parallelism with load balancing for the MoE layers, an asynchronous batch scheduler turned on by default, and deterministic, batch-invariant sampling on Nvidia hardware. Structured output supports regex, JSON schema and EBNF grammars.

It runs exactly one model today, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, with the 1017 checkpoint as the default. DeepSeek says future models will be added as they ship.

What's not in it is the more telling list. The README says the release is offline inference only and explicitly excludes the KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation, and data-parallel load balancing. Those three are most of what makes a large-scale serving deployment cheap.

DeepSeek said back in 2025 that it wouldn't open its full engine as a single repo and would push components upstream instead, and DeepInfer is consistent with that: a very good single-node reference, not the thing actually running DeepSeek's API.

Hardware support is the other signal. The supported targets are Nvidia SM100 parts on CUDA 13 and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs on CANN 9.2. No Hopper, no consumer cards, and Ascend as a first-class target rather than an afterthought port.

That matches where DeepSeek has said its compute is going, and it means the repo is more immediately useful to a Chinese cloud running Ascend than to a US startup with a rack of H100s.

The pricing context is why anyone outside the inference-kernel crowd cares. OpenRouter lists V4.1-Flash at $0.035 per million input tokens and $0.12 per million output. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra is listed at $10 and $50 for the same. That's not a like-for-like comparison, since the models aren't in the same class, but it's the gap DeepSeek is pointing at when it talks about lowering compute costs.

The benchmarks DeepInfer publishes are prefill and decode Pareto curves measured on 4 and 64 SM100 GPUs respectively, with no absolute throughput numbers in the text, so treat the efficiency claims as directional until someone outside DeepSeek reproduces them.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Models Land on Google Cloud, the Last Hyperscaler Without Them
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are in private preview in Google Cloud's Model Garden, billed on the customer's existing Google invoice, with general availability promised in the coming weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Google Cloud now sells OpenAI. As of October 21, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are available in Model Garden as a private preview for selected enterprise customers, with OpenAI saying general availability is weeks away. Everyone else can fill in an interest form.

The models are positioned the way OpenAI positions them elsewhere: Astra for demanding coding, computer-use and research work, Sol as the cheaper option with most of Astra's capability, Luna for fast, high-volume routine tasks.

Eligible customers can hit them through the API today and can point local Codex CLI and Codex Desktop sessions at Google's inference. Gemini for business and the Antigravity coding environment get them later. Zero Data Retention and Confidential Compute are listed as coming soon, which enterprise security teams will correctly read as "not yet."

The commercial mechanics matter more than the model list. Usage lands on the customer's existing Google Cloud invoice, draws down committed spend, and counts toward Flexible Savings Plans alongside Gemini and Anthropic usage. That's the whole pitch: a procurement team that already has a Google commit no longer needs a separate OpenAI contract to use GPT-6.

Michael Gerstenhaber, VP of product management at Google Cloud, framed it as matching each workload to the right model. Google's own post goes further and claims it's now the only hyperscaler offering all three leading closed-source model families.

That claim is Google's, and it's narrowly true. Microsoft sells OpenAI and, more recently, Anthropic. AWS sells Anthropic and has carried OpenAI models since summer 2025. Neither sells Gemini.

GPT models were Azure-only for years because of Microsoft's investment. That exclusivity has been eroding for a while, first with AWS and now with Google, and Google was the obvious last stop.

The more interesting question is what Microsoft gets out of the relationship now that its position as OpenAI's exclusive cloud is fully gone. The answer is probably the revenue share and the Azure consumption, which were always the point, but the marketing story is over.

For developers already on Vertex AI, the practical change is a model switch rather than a platform switch. For OpenAI, it's distribution into the accounts Google has been winning with Gemini. Watch the per-token pricing when GA lands. Google hasn't published any yet, and whether GPT-6 on Google costs the same as GPT-6 on OpenAI's own API will tell you who's subsidizing whom.

item.title: Tesla's Q3: Flat Revenue, Profit Down 43%, and Capex at Half of Plan
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Tesla booked $28.05 billion in revenue and $787 million in GAAP net income for the quarter, with AI and Optimus spending outrunning gross profit and nine-month capex at $13 billion against a full-year guide of more than $25 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla's third quarter was flat on top and down hard underneath. Revenue came in at $28.05 billion, essentially unchanged from a year ago and in line with what Wall Street expected. GAAP net income fell 43% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share. Operating income dropped 56% to $718 million, a 2.6% operating margin, which the company attributes to AI and Optimus spending growing faster than gross profit.

The margin story is better than the profit story. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% a year ago, and automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits climbed to 18.1% from 15.4%. Those credits, which propped up many a Tesla quarter, shrank 73% to $113 million.

Services and other revenue grew 33% to $4.61 billion. Energy generation and storage went the other way, down 16% to $2.88 billion even as deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh, which means pricing in that business is sliding.

Deliveries were 486,532, down about 2% year over year. Production was 464,391.

Tesla's explanation for the flat volume is new: battery availability "continued to be the limiting factor in increasing auto volumes in the quarter." That's a supply constraint. Falling average selling prices are a demand signal. Both showing up in the same quarter doesn't quite add up, and the shareholder letter doesn't try to reconcile them.

Then there's capex. Tesla spent $4.73 billion in the quarter, down from $5.79 billion in Q2, bringing the nine-month total to $13.01 billion. Management guided the year to "more than $25 billion" and didn't update that number.

Either the fourth quarter absorbs roughly $12 billion of spending, or a chunk of the 2026 plan (Optimus production lines, Cybercab capacity, the Terafab chip project) is quietly sliding into 2027. The lower spend is also why free cash flow looks respectable at $1.53 billion; it's still down 62% from a year ago.

Two line items below the operating line are worth noting. Tesla's bitcoin holdings produced a $288 million unrealized gain, and its SpaceX equity stake produced a $142 million unrealized loss, which together added about $146 million to GAAP net income. Strip them out and the quarter is thinner still.

On the autonomy side, the robotaxi fleet passed nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles by quarter end, with Cybercab joining the Austin service about a month ago. FSD active subscriptions hit 1.74 million, up 67%, though that count includes upfront purchases, so it isn't a recurring-revenue number. The quarter reads as a company whose car business is treading water while its board and its CEO are busy on another question entirely: the SpaceX combination both companies' special committees are now studying.

item.title: A 2012 Test Account With 'Password1' Exposed 3,300 Welsh Children's Records
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The ICO reprimanded IT provider Ogi Networks and Data Cymru after a November 2024 ransomware attack walked in through a 12-year-old Active Directory account that nobody ever removed.
item.content:encoded:
Someone at Ogi Networks created an Active Directory account called Test2 on 13 January 2012. They gave it the password "Password1." Nobody deleted it. In November 2024, an attacker logged in with it, encrypted 182.7 GB across Data Cymru's file servers and SQL database, and walked out with 42 GB that included personal information on about 3,300 people, most of them children.

That's the whole story the UK Information Commissioner's Office told on October 20, when it published reprimands against both Ogi Networks Limited, the IT provider, and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, which trades as Data Cymru and is funded by the Welsh government. The stolen data came from a domain controller, a file server and an SQL server and covered two child and family projects.

The ICO ran the password through a strength tool. It rated "Password1" as very weak and estimated it could be cracked in under a second. The regulator's press release headline was blunt: "'Password1' is not an appropriate password." David Doodson, the ICO's head of investigations, said organisations should remove accounts that are no longer required and block weak, commonly used passwords. Ogi said it accepted the findings and had acted on them.

The ICO found both organisations breached UK GDPR but put more of the fault on Ogi, which created the account, never removed it, and never reviewed local administrator accounts after initial setup. Neither got a fine. Reprimands only.

That's the part worth sitting with. A public body's IT provider left a default-password account live for twelve years, it led to the theft of children's data, and the consequence is a published letter. The ICO has said for a couple of years that it prefers reprimands over fines for public-sector bodies so money isn't pulled from services.

Ogi is a private company, though, and the same leniency applied. Since the attack, Ogi has tightened account access controls and the two organisations have signed a compliant data processing contract, which the reprimand notes they didn't have before.

The practical takeaway is the one every audit framework already has in it and nobody enjoys doing: pull your Active Directory for accounts with no login in a year, accounts with "test" in the name, and accounts created before your current staff joined. Then check which of them still have a password that would fail a 2012 complexity policy. Ogi's did, and the ICO's reprimand will sit on the first page of search results for both companies for years.

item.title: FoxIO Publishes PoC for QPACK Flaws That Crash 7 of 10 HTTP/3 Servers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: FoxIO's Header Accordions research shows tiny compressed header batches expanding thousands of times in memory on quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic and Bun, with fixes out for three stacks and Bun, hyperium h3 and aioquic still open.
item.content:encoded:
Under 10 MiB of traffic across 50 connections. That's what it took in FoxIO's proof-of-concept to push an HTTP/3 server's container to its 5 GiB memory cap in about a second. The write-up, titled Header Accordions, went public on October 20 along with working exploit code, and it found the same flaw class in seven of the ten HTTP/3 implementations the firm tested.

The bug is in how QPACK, HTTP/3's header compression scheme, gets enforced. Most stacks cap the compressed size of a header block on the wire. Fewer cap what that block expands into, or they apply the limit only after the whole thing has been decoded into memory.

FoxIO's first technique exploits that gap directly: on quic-go at default settings, a 1 MB batch unpacked into roughly 160,000 header fields and around 15 MB of resident memory, about 17x amplification. quic-go's own advisory puts the ceiling closer to 50x.

The second technique is nastier. The attacker stores a single header entry of about 4 KB in the dynamic table, then references it over and over with one-byte indexed references. Every reference makes the server rebuild the full entry.

FoxIO measured roughly 4,000x amplification on Bun and 600 to 1,800x on lsquic. Bun has an extra problem on top: a running-total counter overflows past 2 GB and the decoder spins forever, so a single stream of about 516 KB pins a core at 100%.

This is denial of service, not code execution. FoxIO reports no data exposure and no evidence of in-the-wild use.

Patch status is mixed. quic-go fixed it in 0.57.0 (CVE-2025-64702), Cloudflare's quiche in 0.29.3 (CVE-2026-12523), and lsquic in 4.9.0 back in July by capping the unpacked header sets held per stream, though lsquic never issued a CVE.

Wireshark picked up CVE-2025-13945 for a dissector crash, which matters for anyone running packet capture on untrusted traffic but isn't a server-side issue. Bun, hyperium's h3 crate, and aioquic (which mitmproxy depends on) have no fix as of FoxIO's publication. IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3 and Google's quiche were not affected because they count unpacked headers as they decode.

If you run one of the unpatched stacks: don't expose Bun's HTTP/3 server to the internet, start mitmproxy with http3 disabled, and set max_field_section_size on h3. If you run one of the patched ones, this is a plain upgrade. And if you're behind a CDN that terminates HTTP/3 for you, this is a good week to ask which stack they're running.

item.title: Node.js Patches Brotli RCE Reachable Through fetch() in 22, 24 and 26
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in Node's bundled Brotli decoder, fixed in 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1, and any app that decompresses br responses or request bodies is in scope.
item.content:encoded:
Ten CVEs, three release lines, one Wednesday. The Node.js project shipped 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, and the one to care about is CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled into Node itself. The project rates it High and says plainly that it permits remote code execution.

What makes this worse than a typical decoder bug is how little an app has to do to reach it. Node's built-in fetch() transparently decompresses responses tagged Content-Encoding: br. Express 5's body parser decompresses br request bodies by default.

So a service that never imports zlib, never calls brotliDecompress, and never thinks about compression can still hand attacker-controlled bytes to the vulnerable code, either by fetching a hostile URL or by accepting a crafted POST.

Exploitation hasn't been reported. The advisory says nothing about attacks in the wild, no CVSS score is published yet, and the bug isn't on CISA's KEV list. That's today. Decoder memory-corruption bugs with a clear trigger path tend not to stay theoretical.

The other three High-rated fixes are all about identity. CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483 are TLS hostname-verification bypasses (one triggered when a hostname loosely resolves to an IP, the other when an IP is written in fullwidth Unicode digits), and CVE-2026-105482 is a dns.resolve bug that truncates names containing a NUL byte.

Individually they're edge cases. Together they're the kind of thing that turns a certificate check into a suggestion. Three Medium and three Low issues round out the ten, including a randomUUID() entropy-cache bug that makes processes built from startup snapshots or single-executable applications repeat values they should never repeat.

If you're on Node 20 or 25, there's no patch coming. Both lines are end-of-life, and the project's position is that EOL versions are always affected by security releases. That's a bigger population than it sounds. Node 20 was the LTS line a lot of production fleets standardized on, and a fair number of them haven't moved.

Update to the fixed version on your line. If you can't do it today, the narrower mitigations are to strip br from the Accept-Encoding header on outbound fetch() calls and disable br inflation in body parsers until you can. Then go find out which of your containers are still pinned to node:20.

item.title: PHP2Shell: Two 9.2 RCE Bugs Hit Every PHP Since 5.4, Patch Lands Today
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: PHP ships an out-of-cycle fix at 14:00 UTC for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 after exploit code leaked a day early and Cloudflare reported the first attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Every web server running PHP 5.4 or later is exposed to a pair of unauthenticated remote code execution bugs, and the only real fix arrives at 14:00 UTC today. PHP's security team posted the advance notice on Monday, rating both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 at CVSS v4.0 9.2 and promising version details with the release.

By Tuesday night the embargo had collapsed. Someone leaked a screenshot of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, credited to Calif.IO, with a banner claiming it works against every PHP release from 5.4.0 onward.

watchTowr, which had been working under the original embargo, said everyone was supposed to wait until Thursday. The PHP team pulled the release forward to Wednesday instead. watchTowr also says it independently reproduced CVE-2026-109618, which is about as strong a confirmation as you'll get before the patch drops.

The attack surface appears to be multipart form parsing. PHP processes multipart/form-data request bodies before any application code runs, which is why PHP core developers have been blunt that configuration won't save you. Core developer Gina Peter Banyard called patching the only mitigation, and 8.6 release manager Joe Ferguson said flatly that ini settings won't help. Disabling session upload progress does nothing against this.

Exploitation has started. Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said the company was seeing early attacks emerging, and Sansec's timeline puts Cloudflare's first observation at 07:43 UTC on Wednesday, hours before the patch. Nobody has published indicators yet. Sansec, which watches e-commerce platforms like Magento, Shopware, and WooCommerce, expects mass scanning within 15 minutes of the fix going public, because the diff will tell attackers exactly where to aim.

Fixes are coming only for supported branches: 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. Pre-release reporting from Kevin Beaumont points to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 as the fixed builds, but confirm against php.net once the release is live.

PHP 8.1 and everything older is end-of-life and gets nothing official. One estimate puts the count of internet-facing EOL PHP hosts near 884,000. Distribution vendors will backport for the enterprise Linux branches they still support, so check your distro's advisory rather than assuming you're stuck.

If you can't patch in the next few hours, the stopgaps are ugly but real. Block multipart/form-data at nginx or Apache, which also breaks file uploads.

Put the origin behind a WAF (Cloudflare says its managed rules cover the known vectors, free tier included) and lock origin access to the WAF's IP ranges so attackers can't go around it. Or take the site read-only by rejecting anything that isn't GET or HEAD. CERT-EU went further and told members to isolate internet-facing PHP applications until fixed.

One warning: exploit code is circulating on forums and GitHub, and almost none of it is verified. Some of it will be malware aimed at defenders who download it to test. Wait for the official diff.

item.title: eMudhra's CA Keys Could Be Computed From Public Certs. Browsers Pulled Them
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were generated with so little randomness that a researcher recovered every private key in under a second, forcing Chrome, Firefox, Apple, and Microsoft to block them.
item.content:encoded:
Scott Helme recovered all eight private keys in less than a second. He didn't steal them. He computed them from the public certificates, because eMudhra's April 2025 key generation ceremony produced keys with so little entropy that the math falls apart on inspection. Anyone who did the same work could have minted a certificate for any domain on the internet, and Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Windows would have trusted it.

The report came in on Friday, October 17, from a researcher Mozilla credits only as Wayne. Chrome's Root Program had a CRLSet block live within an hour and forty minutes. Mozilla's team recovered the keys themselves within two hours of being notified and had OneCRL pushed by late evening.

Apple blocked the certificates Sunday, Android devices got a block through Play Services Sunday night, and Microsoft followed Monday. Google and Mozilla published their statements Monday too. That's a fast, coordinated response, and it deserves credit.

The eight certificates break down as six TLS intermediates (DV, OV, and EV, each in a G3B and G3C variant) chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, plus two code-signing intermediates. Each also exists as a Sectigo cross-signed copy with the same public key, which is why Chrome blocked by key rather than by certificate. Chrome didn't block the code-signing pair because its TLS verifier won't build a path through a code-signing-restricted intermediate anyway.

eMudhra's account, published Tuesday to the Bombay Stock Exchange, is that the ceremony used FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSMs and a flaw in a key wrap/unwrap step produced a second, weak set of keys alongside the intended strong ones. The weak set is what got published to root stores.

The company says its infrastructure wasn't breached, that only one of the eight was ever deployed in production, that none issued end-entity certificates, and that global TLS is about 1% of its revenue. Its shares dropped roughly 20% in Mumbai anyway.

Here's the problem with the reassurance. No certificate chaining to the six TLS intermediates appears in Certificate Transparency logs before Chrome's block, which is good. But CT only records what's logged, and a forged certificate used in a targeted interception would have no reason to be logged.

Nobody can say whether these keys were abused. eMudhra is also still determining the root cause of a flaw it has already explained, which reads like the explanation arrived before the investigation did.

The browser side is handled for you. The rest of your stack isn't. Go binaries, Python's certifi bundle, Node.js, and most non-browser TLS clients don't check revocation and will trust these chains until their root bundles or code change. Go shipped 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 to reject the eight keys, which requires rebuilding; Go 1.25 and older get nothing.

Node's fix is a draft PR. Cloudflare pushed updated WARP, 1.1.1.1, and cloudflared clients. Chrome removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 entirely in root store version 43, expected to reach devices around October 27, and anyone with a certificate under that root needs a new chain before then.

If you run anything that pins a root bundle, audit it this week.

item.title: Qilin and Inc Ransomware Walk Through a GlobalProtect Bug Patched in May
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Unit 42 says at least two ransomware crews are using CVE-2026-0257, an authentication override cookie flaw in PAN-OS GlobalProtect, to open VPN sessions without credentials and bypass MFA on their way to vCenter.
item.content:encoded:
The bug was rated medium when Palo Alto Networks disclosed it on May 13. Four days later Rapid7 saw attackers using it against customer firewalls.

Five months on, Palo Alto's own Unit 42 team has updated its threat brief to say Qilin and Inc ransomware affiliates are among the groups exploiting it, and ReliaQuest adds Settra to the list. The flaw is CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass in GlobalProtect portals and gateways, and the fix has been available since the day it was disclosed.

The mechanics are embarrassing in the way VPN bugs usually are. GlobalProtect's authentication override feature issues a cookie so users don't have to re-authenticate for a set period. The firewall trusted that cookie without properly validating its integrity, so a remote attacker with no credentials could forge one and establish a VPN session.

MFA never comes into it because the cookie says you already passed. Palo Alto now scores it CVSS 4.0 7.8 with exploit maturity marked as attacked, and its advisory asks for the highest urgency.

What the crews do after they're in is textbook, which is the point. Unit 42 describes attackers using legitimate IT management tools to look around and move laterally, then credential and data theft, then ransomware.

In one case the intruders went from the VPN gateway to the vCenter appliance, disabled security controls on the ESXi hosts, and ran a custom tool against the domain controller's virtual disk to pull credentials offline. Some chained in the old Veeam bug, CVE-2023-27532. ReliaQuest found Cobalt Strike, BloodHound, and SharpHound in its cases. Healthcare, education, government, and energy have all taken hits.

Exposure requires a specific setup: a GlobalProtect portal or gateway with authentication override cookies enabled, plus a particular certificate configuration. That's a real limiter and probably why the initial severity was low. It's also a common enough configuration that two separate ransomware operations built playbooks around it.

Fixed builds span four PAN-OS branches. On 12.1 you need 12.1.4-h6 or 12.1.7; on 11.2, 11.2.4-h17, 11.2.7-h14, 11.2.10-h7, or 11.2.12; on 11.1, 11.1.4-h33, 11.1.6-h32, 11.1.7-h6, 11.1.10-h25, 11.1.13-h5, or 11.1.15; on 10.2, 10.2.7-h34, 10.2.10-h36, 10.2.13-h21, 10.2.16-h7, or 10.2.18-h6. Prisma Access needs 11.2.7-h13 or 10.2.10-h36. Cloud NGFW and Panorama aren't affected. If you can't patch, use a dedicated certificate for authentication override cookies or turn the override options off entirely in the portal and gateway config.

Patching isn't the whole job. ReliaQuest's warning is that access established before remediation survives it. Terminate every active GlobalProtect session after you upgrade, then go through the connection logs for anything you don't recognize.

Unit 42 specifically flags sessions from hosts named "kali," which tells you how little effort some of these operators bother with. ReliaQuest expects the exploitation to run at least another three months, because the install base that hasn't patched in five months isn't going to start now.

item.title: Salesforce Pays $5.66B for Braze to Fix the Marketing Cloud It Already Owns
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Braze shareholders get $47.50 a share in cash, Braze keeps its brand and CEO, and the deal won't close before Salesforce's next fiscal year.
item.content:encoded:
$47.50 a share, all cash, about $5.66 billion in enterprise value. That's what Salesforce agreed Monday to pay for Braze, the customer engagement platform that sends the push notifications, in-app messages, SMS, WhatsApp, and email that brands like Instacart, Venmo, Canva, and Dairy Queen fire at their customers. Braze stock jumped around 50% on the news, which tells you roughly how far below that price it had been trading.

Salesforce already sells this. Marketing Cloud has been in the portfolio since the ExactTarget deal in 2013, and the company has spent a decade bolting acquisitions onto it. Buying Braze is an admission that the real-time, event-driven side of the product never caught up with the specialists.

Braze was built on a streaming architecture that reacts to what a user just did inside an app, and that's precisely the capability Salesforce needs if Agentforce is going to do anything useful in consumer marketing beyond drafting copy.

The official framing is that Braze complements all four layers of the Salesforce stack: Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce. Strip the branding and it means Braze's decisioning engine gets wired to Salesforce's customer data and agent layer. Braze will keep its name and CEO Bill Magnuson stays on with his leadership team. It has about 2,770 customers and 15 offices.

The price is steep by Salesforce's own numbers. The company said it's paying roughly five times Braze's expected fiscal 2028 revenue, and outside estimates put it near eight times trailing revenue.

Salesforce says it expects the deal to add to growth but dilute profitability in the near term, and that it doesn't need debt to fund it. Fiscal 2027 guidance is unchanged. The deal closes in fiscal 2028, which starts in February, and only after Braze shareholders and regulators sign off.

Regulators are the open question. Salesforce and Braze are two of the larger vendors of brand-to-consumer messaging, and consolidation in martech has gone mostly unchallenged for years. This is a big enough check, in a category with few remaining independents, that someone in Washington or Brussels may at least ask.

For teams running Braze today, nothing changes for at least four months. After that, expect the Salesforce sales motion to show up in your renewal conversation.
